claim: The novel highly infectious severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) spread rapidly around the world in the first months of 2020.
source: Starting in Wuhan, China, the novel highly infectious severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) spread rapidly around the world in the first months of 2020 and was declared as a pandemic by the WHO on 13 March 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the spread of COVID-19 that is part of established scientific and historical record.

claim: COVID-19 was declared as a pandemic by the WHO on 13 March 2020.
source: Starting in Wuhan, China, the novel highly infectious severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2, COVID-19) spread rapidly around the world in the first months of 2020 and was declared as a pandemic by the WHO on 13 March 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement citing a specific date for the WHO pandemic declaration.

evidence: This is a speculative statement indicated by 'may have led to'.

claim: Experts expressed concern that fear of contracting SARS-CoV-2 and pandemic-related stressors posed a risk for mental health.
source: Early on, experts expressed concern that the fear of contracting the infection with SARS-CoV-2 as well as pandemic related stressors such as social restrictions, financial preoccupations, task overload, inadequate information, frustration, and boredom posed a risk for mental health, and may be reflected in particular in depressive and anxiety-related symptoms (Amsalem et al., 2021; Brooks et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Amsalem et al., 2021; Brooks et al., 2020).

claim: Pandemic-related stressors may be reflected in particular in depressive and anxiety-related symptoms.
source: Early on, experts expressed concern that the fear of contracting the infection with SARS-CoV-2 as well as pandemic related stressors such as social restrictions, financial preoccupations, task overload, inadequate information, frustration, and boredom posed a risk for mental health, and may be reflected in particular in depressive and anxiety-related symptoms (Amsalem et al., 2021; Brooks et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Amsalem et al., 2021; Brooks et al., 2020).

claim: Social distancing measures represent a macro-stressor affecting the majority of people in an unprecedented manner.
source: Social distancing measures in particular represent a macro-stressor affecting the majority of people in an unprecedented manner (Ahrens et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Ahrens et al., 2021).

claim: Severe restrictions of social contacts and fear of the virus had a measurable impact on the mental health of general populations worldwide.
source: Different studies indeed showed that severe restrictions of social contacts as well as the fear of the virus or the impact on living conditions had a measurable impact on the mental health of general populations all over the world (Bu et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Bu et al., 2020; Smith et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020b).

claim: During the first lockdown, increased levels of perceived stress, mental distress, COVID-19 related fear, general anxiety and depression, and a general decline in mental well-being were observed in many countries, including Germany and the UK.
source: During the first lockdown, increased levels of perceived stress and mental distress, COVID-19 related fear, general anxiety and depression, and a general decline in mental well-being were observed in many countries, including Germany and the UK (Bäuerle et al., 2020; Fancourt et al., 2021; Proto and Quintana-Domeque, 2021; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Bäuerle et al., 2020; Fancourt et al., 2021; Proto and Quintana-Domeque, 2021; Smith et al., 2020).

claim: There is a risk that people engage more in unhealthy behaviour and coping strategies during the pandemic, such as excessive consumption of alcohol or drugs.
source: In this stressful context, there is the additional risk that people engage more in unhealthy behaviour and coping strategies, such as excessive consumption of alcohol or drugs, potentially due to insecurity and social restrictions (Clay and Parker, 2020; Marsden et al., 2020; McKay and Asmundson, 2020; Pfefferbaum and North, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Clay and Parker, 2020; Marsden et al., 2020; McKay and Asmundson, 2020; Pfefferbaum and North, 2020).

claim: In the week ending 21 March, alcohol sales in UK supermarkets rose by 67%.
source: In the week ending 21 March , alcohol sales rose by 67%, but total supermarket sales increased by only 43% (Finlay and Gilmore, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Finlay and Gilmore, 2020).

claim: Total supermarket sales in the UK increased by only 43% in the week ending 21 March.
source: In the week ending 21 March , alcohol sales rose by 67%, but total supermarket sales increased by only 43% (Finlay and Gilmore, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Finlay and Gilmore, 2020).

claim: Some studies reported an increase in alcohol consumption in one fifth to one third of participants during the first weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic in spring 2020.
source: Some studies reported an increase in alcohol consumption in one fifth to one third of the participants during the first weeks of the COVID-19 pandemic in spring 2020 (Daly and Robinson, 2021; Jacob et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Daly and Robinson, 2021; Jacob et al., 2021; Taylor et al., 2021).

claim: A study in 21 European countries showed that alcohol consumption generally decreased in all countries except for the UK, where alcohol consumption increased, and Ireland, where consumption remained the same.
source: A study in 21 European countries showed that alcohol consumption generally decreased in all countries except for the UK, where alcohol consumption increased, and Ireland, where consumption remained the same (Kilian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Kilian et al., 2021).

claim: Particular groups are at increased risk of alcohol consumption changes during the pandemic, including individuals with children and those with higher depressive or anxiety scores.
source: However, the literature shows that the patterns of alcohol consumption change in the course of the pandemic, that is, fewer episodes of heavy drinking (Kilian et al., 2021), but also that particular groups are at increased risk, for example, individuals with children, and those with higher depressive or anxiety scores (Sallie et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Kilian et al., 2021; Sallie et al., 2020).

claim: While the normal population did not increase their drinking behaviour, those who already showed harmful or problematic drinking patterns increased their consumption.
source: Marsden and colleagues showed that while the normal population did not increase their drinking behaviour, those who already showed harmful or problematic drinking patterns increased their consumption (Marsden et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Marsden et al., 2020).

claim: The consumption of other substances, including legal, illegal, and prescriptive drugs, may have increased in response to the pandemic in general.
source: The consumption of other substances, including legal, illegal, and prescriptive drugs, may also have increased in response to the pandemic in general (Manthey et al., 2021), and specifically to cope with COVID-19 related stress (Czeisler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Manthey et al., 2021; Czeisler et al., 2020).

claim: People with a substance use disorder may increase their consumption in reaction to the negative impact of the pandemic situation.
source: People with a substance use disorder may increase their consumption in reaction to the negative impact of the situation, shift to other substances if access to their primary substances becomes limited, or relapse if they have already recovered from the addiction (Chiappini et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Chiappini et al., 2020).

claim: The media plays a particular role in how individuals cope with disasters.
source: Besides substance use, many people may also 'escape' from the current situation through excessive media consumption or use media excessively in search for information regarding the current situation. The media plays a particular role in how individuals cope with disasters (Taylor, 2019), which also applies to the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Taylor, 2019).

claim: The WHO recently started using the term 'infodemic' in the context of the COVID-19 crisis.
source: Interestingly, the WHO recently started using the term 'infodemic' in the context of the present crisis as 'a tsunami of misinformation, hate, scapegoating, and scare-mongering (which) has been unleashed' (WHO, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (WHO, 2020).

claim: Excessive media consumption (>3 hr daily) is associated with poorer mental health.
source: A large body of literature suggests that excessive media consumption (>3 hr daily) is associated with poorer mental health (Abbas et al., 2021; Bendau et al., 2021 Gao et al., 2020; Neophytou et al., 2019; Ni et al., 2020; Su et al., 2021; Valdez et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a; Zendle, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple external sources (Abbas et al., 2021; Bendau et al., 2021 Gao et al., 2020; Neophytou et al., 2019; Ni et al., 2020; Su et al., 2021; Valdez et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a; Zendle, 2020).

claim: Previous studies indicated an increase in schizotypic traits during the pandemic.
source: Our previous studies indicated an increase in schizotypic traits during the pandemic (Daimer et al., 2021; Knolle et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Daimer et al., 2021; Knolle et al., 2021).

claim: Schizotypy describes a multidimensional unifying construct that represents the underlying vulnerability for schizophrenia-spectrum psychopathology.
source: Schizotypy describes a multidimensional unifying construct that represents the underlying vulnerability for schizophrenia-spectrum psychopathology that is expressed across a broad range of personality, subclinical, and clinical psychosis phenomenology (Debbané and Barrantes-Vidal, 2015; Grant and Hennig, 2020; Raine, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Debbané and Barrantes-Vidal, 2015; Grant and Hennig, 2020; Raine, 1991).

claim: Schizotypy is regarded as a latent multidimensional personality trait that occurs in varying degrees in every person along a continuum.
source: It is regarded as a latent multidimensional personality trait that occurs in varying degrees in every person along a continuum (Grant et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Grant et al., 2018).

claim: All definitions of schizotypy include positive (e.g. paranoia), negative (i.e. lack of trust), and disorganised traits, similar to schizophrenia.
source: There is no consensus on the exact content of the construct, but all definitions include positive (e.g. paranoia), negative (i.e. lack of trust), and disorganised traits, similar to schizophrenia (Wright et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Wright et al., 2011).

claim: Paranoia related to the risk of a contagious virus may result in individuals experiencing higher levels of psychological stress, depressive feelings, and anxiety.
source: For example, paranoia related to the risk of a contagious virus may result in individuals experiencing higher levels of psychological stress, depressive feelings, and anxiety (Preti et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Preti et al., 2020).

claim: People scoring high on schizotypy were more likely to think they had COVID-19 symptoms than people with low schizotypy.
source: Fekih-Romdhane and colleagues showed that people scoring high on schizotypy were more likely to think they had COVID-19 symptoms than people with low schizotypy, and they also experienced more pronounced fear of illness (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).

claim: People scoring high on schizotypy experienced more pronounced fear of illness during the pandemic.
source: Fekih-Romdhane and colleagues showed that people scoring high on schizotypy were more likely to think they had COVID-19 symptoms than people with low schizotypy, and they also experienced more pronounced fear of illness (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).

claim: Individuals with low schizotypy had a variety of strategies to adaptively cope with the fear of COVID-19.
source: Furthermore, a comparison between individuals with low and high schizotypy during the pandemic showed that those with low schizotypy had a variety of strategies to adaptively cope with the fear of COVID-19 (e.g. positive reframing, planning, religion, self-distraction, and behavioural disengagement), yet those with high schizotypy had fewer such strategies (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).

claim: Those with high schizotypy were more likely to use maladaptive strategies such as venting or self-blame.
source: Those with high schizotypy were more likely to use maladaptive strategies such as venting or self-blame, which were less effective in reducing COVID-19 related anxiety (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an external source (Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021).

claim: Individuals with high schizotypal traits have fewer and poorer social contacts compared to others.
source: Due to greater levels of introversion and mistrust of others, individuals with high schizotypal traits have fewer and poorer social contacts compared to others, are less integrated into communities, and are more likely to be lonely (Kozloff et al., 2020; Le et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Kozloff et al., 2020; Le et al., 2019).

claim: Individuals with high schizotypal traits are less integrated into communities and are more likely to be lonely.
source: Due to greater levels of introversion and mistrust of others, individuals with high schizotypal traits have fewer and poorer social contacts compared to others, are less integrated into communities, and are more likely to be lonely (Kozloff et al., 2020; Le et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to external sources (Kozloff et al., 2020; Le et al., 2019).

claim: Individuals with high schizotypal traits may be particularly likely to succumb to media misinformation due to their low agreeableness and disposition towards believing conspiracist ideation.
source: Additionally, individuals with high schizotypal traits may be particularly likely to succumb to media misinformation, for example, due to their low agreeableness (Kwapil et al., 2018) and disposition towards believing conspiracist ideation (Barron et al., 2014).

source: Exploring the effect of 'social adversity' on schizotypy (Figure 5, Table 5), we found that in all four surveys, social adversity was associated with higher levels of schizotypal traits, with this association being most pronounced in the May 2021 survey (c=0.33).

claim: The mediation of the effect of COVID-19 concerns on SPQ via media consumption was significant in the January/February 2021 survey.

evidence: This is a direct report of the results from the structural equation modeling analysis.

claim: Media consumption explained a quarter of the total effects of COVID-19 stress on SPQ in the January/February 2021 survey.

claim: A significant indirect effect with the mediator excessive media consumption was seen in January/February 2021: 12.5% of the effects of COVID-19 related concerns on anxiety symptoms occurred through excessive media consumption.
